subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What are the products when calcium reacts with cold water?
questions.explain: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2; Group 2 metals form the hydroxide and hydrogen gas with water.

questions.q: Adding NaOH(aq) to Fe3+(aq) produces a precipitate that is:
questions.explain: Fe3+ forms a red-brown gelatinous precipitate of Fe(OH)3.

questions.q: Why does sodium have a much lower melting point than aluminium in Period 3?
options: Sodium is a giant covalent structure
Aluminium delocalises three electrons per atom and has a higher charge density, giving stronger metallic bonding
Aluminium has weaker metallic bonding due to its larger ions
questions.explain: Al3+ has a smaller ion and contributes three delocalised electrons, so its metallic bonding is much stronger than that of Na, raising the melting point.

questions.q: The relationship between the energy gap and the frequency of light absorbed by a complex is given by:
questions.explain: The d-orbital splitting energy equals Planck's constant times the frequency of the absorbed light, dE = h x frequency.

questions.q: Why does the melting point fall sharply between silicon and phosphorus in Period 3?
options: Phosphorus is a metal and silicon is not
The structure changes from giant covalent (Si) to simple molecular (P4), so only weak van der Waals forces are broken on melting phosphorus
Phosphorus has stronger covalent bonds than silicon
questions.explain: Silicon's giant covalent lattice requires breaking many strong bonds, whereas molecular P4 needs only weak London forces overcome, giving a sharp drop.

questions.q: Which best explains the general decrease in atomic radius across Period 3 from Na to Ar?
options: Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell of electrons closer; shielding stays roughly constant
The number of neutrons decreases across the period
Shielding increases faster than nuclear charge
Electrons are added to new shells, increasing the radius
questions.explain: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding, so the outer electrons are pulled in and the radius decreases.

questions.q: How does the oxidising ability of the halogens change down Group 7?
questions.explain: Oxidising ability decreases down Group 7 because larger atoms gain an electron less readily, so chlorine is a stronger oxidant than iodine.

questions.q: Which observation correctly identifies the result of adding silver nitrate to a solution containing iodide ions?
options: Yellow precipitate, insoluble in concentrated ammonia
Cream precipitate, soluble in concentrated ammonia
White precipitate, soluble in dilute ammonia
questions.explain: Iodide gives a yellow AgI precipitate that does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia.

questions.q: In the test for halide ions, which precipitate colour confirms a bromide ion when silver nitrate solution is added?
questions.explain: AgBr forms a cream precipitate, between the white of AgCl and the yellow of AgI.

questions.q: When chlorine is added to cold dilute sodium hydroxide, what type of reaction occurs and what are the products?
options: Disproportionation, giving NaCl, NaClO and water
questions.explain: Cl2 + 2NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO + H2O; chlorine is simultaneously oxidised (to +1 in ClO-) and reduced (to -1 in Cl-), so it disproportionates.

questions.q: Why is acidified barium chloride solution used to test for sulfate ions, and why is magnesium hydroxide used in medicine?
options: BaSO4 is soluble; Mg(OH)2 is a strong acid
BaSO4 forms a white precipitate as it is insoluble; Mg(OH)2 is a sparingly soluble base used as an antacid
BaSO4 is green; Mg(OH)2 is a strong oxidiser
Both compounds are soluble and coloured
questions.explain: The insolubility of BaSO4 gives a white precipitate confirming sulfate, while sparingly soluble Mg(OH)2 neutralises stomach acid as 'milk of magnesia'.

questions.q: Silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3. Why?
options: It has the strongest van der Waals forces
It is a metal with very strong metallic bonds
It has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure with strong Si-Si bonds throughout
questions.explain: Silicon forms a giant covalent lattice in which many strong Si-Si covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

questions.q: What type of ligand is the ethanedioate (oxalate) ion, C2O4 2-?
questions.explain: Ethanedioate donates two lone pairs from two oxygen atoms, making it a bidentate ligand.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the increasing reducing power of the halide ions?
questions.explain: Reducing power increases down the group as the larger ions lose their outer electron more readily, so I- is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.q: Why is [CuCl4]2- tetrahedral whereas [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is octahedral?
options: Chloride ions are larger and fewer can fit around the central ion
questions.explain: The larger chloride ligands mean only four can coordinate, giving a coordination number of 4 and a tetrahedral shape.

questions.q: In the reaction Cl2 + H2O gives HCl + HClO, what are the oxidation states of chlorine in the products?
questions.explain: Chlorine is reduced to -1 in HCl and oxidised to +1 in HClO, a disproportionation of chlorine (0) used in water treatment.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxide is added to fields by farmers. What is its main agricultural use?
options: To neutralise acidic soils (raise the pH)
questions.explain: Ca(OH)2 is a base used to neutralise acidic soils, raising their pH.

questions.q: The substitution of six water ligands in [Co(H2O)6]2+ by ethane-1,2-diamine is favourable largely because of the chelate effect, which is driven by:
options: A large decrease in enthalpy only
An increase in entropy as more free particles are released
questions.explain: Replacing many monodentate ligands with fewer multidentate ones increases the number of free particles, giving a positive entropy change.

questions.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the test for halide ions?
options: To remove carbonate or hydroxide ions that would otherwise give a false precipitate
To increase the solubility of the silver halides
To reduce the silver ions to silver
questions.explain: Acidifying with nitric acid removes interfering ions such as carbonate and hydroxide that would form precipitates with silver nitrate.

questions.q: Why does sulfur (S8) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P4) in Period 3?
options: Sulfur has stronger covalent bonds within its molecules
S8 molecules are larger than P4 molecules, giving stronger van der Waals forces between them
Sulfur is a giant covalent structure
questions.explain: Both are simple molecular solids, but the larger S8 molecule has more electrons and stronger London (van der Waals) forces than P4, so it melts at a higher temperature.

questions.q: Which Group 2 metal reacts most vigorously with water?
questions.explain: Reactivity with water increases down Group 2, so barium reacts most vigorously of these.

questions.q: Transition metals and their compounds often make good catalysts because they can:
options: Provide variable oxidation states and surfaces to adsorb reactants
questions.explain: Variable oxidation states allow electron transfer in homogeneous catalysis, while metal surfaces adsorb reactants in heterogeneous catalysis.

questions.q: In the Haber process, iron acts as a:
questions.explain: Solid iron catalyses the gaseous N2/H2 reaction at its surface, a different phase from the reactants, so it is heterogeneous.

questions.q: When NaOH(aq) is added to Al3+(aq) and then in excess, the observation is:
options: A white precipitate that dissolves in excess to a colourless solution
A blue precipitate that dissolves to deep blue
questions.explain: Al(OH)3 is amphoteric; it forms a white precipitate that redissolves in excess NaOH as [Al(OH)4]-.

questions.q: When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium iodide, why are products such as H2S and I2 formed?
options: The reaction is a simple neutralisation
Iodide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce sulfur from +6 to -2
Sulfuric acid acts only as an acid
questions.explain: Iodide is a powerful reducing agent and reduces sulfur in H2SO4 all the way to H2S (and gives I2), unlike chloride which only gives HCl.

questions.q: Why is MgO only slightly soluble and weakly alkaline in water compared with Na2O?
options: MgO does not contain oxide ions
Mg2+ has a higher charge density and MgO has stronger ionic bonding, limiting its reaction with water
questions.explain: The stronger lattice and higher charge density of Mg2+ make MgO sparingly soluble, giving only a weakly alkaline suspension (about pH 9-10).

questions.q: Why is barium more reactive than calcium toward water?
options: Barium has fewer protons than calcium
Calcium has a larger atomic radius than barium
Barium has a higher first ionisation energy so reacts faster
Barium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily, making it more reactive
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are further out and more shielded, lowering ionisation energy, so barium loses electrons (and reacts) more readily than calcium.

questions.q: Aluminium oxide, Al2O3, is classified as amphoteric because it:
options: Reacts with both acids and bases
questions.explain: Al2O3 reacts with acids (forming Al3+ salts) and with alkalis (forming aluminate), so it is amphoteric.

questions.q: What is observed when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
options: The mixture darkens/turns brown as iodine is displaced
questions.explain: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it displaces iodine: Br2 + 2I- gives 2Br- + I2, producing a brown solution.

questions.q: Why does argon have the lowest melting point in Period 3?
options: It has a giant covalent structure
It exists as single atoms with only very weak van der Waals forces between them
questions.explain: Argon is monatomic, so only very weak London forces act between atoms, requiring little energy to melt.
